Nick Boyle: Boyle gives Michigan an advanced processor with two productive seasons in a pro-style offense. He reads the defense before the snap and can change the call to give his offense a favorable look. That command puts him at the top of the preseason quarterback class.
Dannie Montano: Montano pairs a strong arm with outstanding production on throws outside the pocket. The North Dakota State quarterback can move away from pressure and still find a target downfield, giving his offense options when the original play changes. His ability to create on the move sets him apart.
Micah Howard: Howard reads routes early and can mirror receivers step for step through their breaks. Stanford’s corner pairs elite recognition with the movement to stay attached in coverage, giving the defense a shutdown option on the perimeter. He enters the season among the class’s premier non-quarterback prospects.
Dylan Smith: Smith gives Georgia a 6-foot-5 defensive lineman whose size and athletic tools stand out even in a talented front. His productive season shows what that combination can do on the field. He enters the year with the potential to be one of the class’s defining defensive prospects.
Trey Sternberg: Sternberg brings two very different kinds of trouble to an interior defender. Iowa’s guard plays with the edge to set a physical tone in the run game, then settles into elite pass protection. That combination gives an offense a formidable presence inside.
Jaylen Scruggs: A defender can have Scruggs surrounded and still struggle to get a hand on him. Alabama’s dynamic receiver combines elite speed with sudden changes of direction, giving an offense a playmaker who can create space in the tightest situations and threaten from anywhere.
Ramello Williams: Williams comes off the edge with more than one way to reach the quarterback. The Texas rusher brings a broad menu of moves and two seasons of sack and pressure production, giving offensive tackles plenty to prepare for as another year approaches.
Tremon Henderson II: Henderson has the size and coverage tools to make an entire side of the field feel smaller. Clemson’s corner brings the physical skill set to take on demanding assignments, giving scouts a defender to watch closely as the new season unfolds.
Tyler Smit: Smit gives Indiana a downfield target who can win before the ball is snapped and after it arrives. The big receiver pairs an elite release with contested-catch ability and a nose for the end zone, making him a dangerous vertical option.
Amani Okonkwo: Okonkwo brings a track star’s speed and a sturdy frame to the Ole Miss passing game. He can get behind corners in a hurry, then use his strength to bounce off contact, giving an offense a compact deep threat with explosive potential.
Jake Rosario: Michigan can move Rosario around the formation without taking him out of the play. His reliable hands make him a natural receiving option from several alignments, and he has shown he can deliver the block that springs an explosive gain.
Judah Dickinson: Florida’s run game can follow Dickinson when it needs movement up front. One of the strongest players in the class, he uses powerful hands to take control of defenders and drive them off the line, opening room for the back to work.
Malik Smith: Smith reads the run quickly and meets the ball carrier with force. The LSU linebacker puts those instincts on tape consistently, and the way he diagnoses plays gives him the early profile of a player who could lead a defense.
Brayan Myles: Myles has a case as the fastest corner in the class, and that speed shows up against bigger receivers. Michigan’s corner can stay in phase when routes go vertical and has the competitiveness to contest catches against players with a reach advantage.
Ja'Kylan Edwards: Georgia’s Edwards can disrupt a route before the receiver has taken two steps. His size and play strength make him a natural press corner, and his ability to land a firm jam can throw off the timing of a passing concept.
Kentrell Williams: Williams gives Arkansas a physical target who can stretch a defense vertically. The former track athlete gets downfield quickly and finishes deep go balls, a combination that gives him a chance to develop into the featured receiver in a passing game.
Saka Joseph: Joseph broke through at Missouri after beginning his career at Alabama. His athleticism gives him a different gear as an interior pass rusher, and his emergence with the Tigers shows the impact he can make when he gets room to attack a gap and close on the passer.
Jake Denney: Denney carried five-star pedigree into his first season as a starter at Notre Dame before transferring to Texas. The 6-foot-3 quarterback brings good size, arm strength and the mobility to threaten outside the pocket. Those traits give a passing offense room to work on the move.
Jaishawn Brown: Brown gives Notre Dame the size of a power back and the open-field moves to make defenders miss. The 6-foot-2 runner reads space well and can choose between setting up a cut and lowering his pads when a defender closes.
Mosi Sidi: Sidi came to football late after standing out on the high school track. Miami can use his speed in several offensive packages, and he already offers a clear role in the return game with the ability to handle both kicks and punts.
Ron Hopkins: Hopkins came to Ohio State with a strong recruiting résumé and has found ways to produce in a crowded offense. The physical slot receiver brings solid tape into the season, with his work inside giving scouts a clear role to evaluate.
Arvydas Miliauskas: At 25, Miliauskas brings a veteran presence to Purdue’s defensive front. His technique puts him among the most effective pass rushers in the country, and his ability to win with that polish gives scouts a clear reason to keep watching this season.
Markus Saylor Jr: Saylor gives LSU a big target who can stretch the field and create yards after the catch. He can secure the ball, make a quick move and get upfield, an unusual combination of size and shiftiness among this class’s deep threats.
Khassim Hayes: Hayes brings the speed and bend to win around the outside shoulder of a tackle. Clemson’s edge rusher can change direction without giving up much momentum, which lets him take advantage when a blocker struggles to turn and run with him.
Jean-Luc Toussaint: Toussaint began as a three-star safety recruit at Arizona State and moved to corner after transferring to Oregon. The coverage skills have translated, and his 6-foot-4 frame and vertical burst give him the reach to contest throws above the rim.
Zaire Rollins: Rollins fits the profile of a linebacker who can stay on the field as offenses spread out. The Washington defender brings the athleticism to cover ground and the physical tools to give scouts confidence that his game can carry to the next level.
Jaiden Staples-Harris: A former five-star recruit, Staples-Harris enters the season with one productive year at Tennessee and a strong case as the class’s most physically gifted back. He pairs good vision with a sharp juke and gives the offense another option as a receiver.
Xander Haynes: Haynes anchors a strong Iowa front with the base strength to hold his ground and plug interior gaps. That ability makes it hard for runners to find a clear path through the middle and gives the defense a dependable presence against the run.
Eric Fahey: Fahey gives Michigan a dependable target when the offense needs to move the chains. He finds open space consistently and has some of the best hands in the class, putting him in the early first-round conversation among tight ends who can contribute as receivers.
Conner McPherson: McPherson arrives at Texas A&M after making his name at Iowa State. The 6-foot-5 linebacker brings size to the middle of the Aggies’ defense and enters the season in the conversation for the best player at his position nationally as he takes on a new team.
Davion Lee: Lee brings burst and quick changes of direction to Utah’s edge. He can threaten a tackle’s outside shoulder and redirect when the blocker tries to take away that path. A larger role gives him a stage to turn those movement skills into more plays this season.
Matt Osborne: Osborne gives Wisconsin a nose tackle who can hold the middle of the line together. He stands his ground at the point of attack and tackles well when the runner comes through his gap, making him a dependable piece of the run defense.
